full.title: Loved, Sent, Believed

opening.text: Some verses are so familiar that we stop hearing them. These three verses tell us what God felt, what God did, and what it means for anyone who believes. Read them slowly, with four old teachers beside you.

flow.text: The passage begins with love, and Matthew Henry will not let us hurry past it. He wants us to stop and wonder.

flow.work: Matthew Henry's Commentary on the Whole Bible
flow.text: Behold, and wonder, that the *great God* should love such a *worthless* world! That the *holy God* should love such a *wicked* world with a love of good will, when he could not look upon it with any complacency.
Albert Barnes asks what kind of love this is. God does not approve of sin, but he still wants good for sinners.

This does not mean that God approved the conduct of men, but that he had benevolent feelings toward them, or was earnestly desirous of their happiness. God hates wickedness, but he still desires the happiness of those who are sinful. He hates the sin, but loves the sinner.
And Calvin reminds us that nothing in us earned it.

Nor does he say that God was moved to deliver us, because he perceived in us something that was worthy of so excellent a blessing, but ascribes the glory of our deliverance entirely to his love. And this is still more clear from what follows; for he adds, that God gave his Son to men, that they may not perish.
If God sent his Son, why did he send him? These verses tell us: not to judge, but to save. Augustine pictures a doctor at the bedside.

"For God sent not His Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world through Him may be saved." So far, then, as it lies in the physician, He is come to heal the sick. He that will not observe the orders of the physician destroys himself. He is come a Saviour to the world: why is he called the Saviour of the world, but that He is come to save the world, not to judge the world?
Matthew Henry hears the question every guilty heart asks when heaven comes near: is it peace?

flow.work: Matthew Henry's Commentary on the Whole Bible
flow.text: Ever since man sinned, he has dreaded the approach and appearance of any special messenger from heaven, as being conscious of guilt and looking for judgment: *We shall surely die, for we have seen God.* If therefore the Son of God himself come, we are concerned to enquire on what errand he comes: *Is it peace?* Or, as they asked Samuel trembling, *Comest thou peaceably?* And this scripture returns the answer, *Peaceably.*
The last verse draws the line. Jamieson, Fausset and Brown put the two sides plainly.

flow.work: Commentary Critical and Explanatory on the Whole Bible
flow.text:
18. is not condemned—Having, immediately on his believing, "passed from death unto life" (Joh 5:24).
condemned already—Rejecting the one way of deliverance from that "condemnation" which God gave His Son to remove, and so wilfully remaining condemned.
So the door is open, and the gift is already given. Believing is how we walk through.

road.scripture: But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.
road.text: Romans 5:8 makes the same point from another side: God showed his love while we were still sinners. Henry marks how great that love is. Coming back to John 3:16, we see that the world God loved was not a good world waiting to be rewarded.
road.prompt: Where do you still feel you have to earn God's love?

quotes.work: Matthew Henry's Commentary on the Whole Bible
quotes.text: Some think he alludes to a common distinction the Jews had of their people into *ndyqym*—*righteous,* *hsdym*—*merciful* (compare Isa 17:1), and *rssym*—*wicked.* Now herein *God commended his love,* not only proved or evidenced his love (he might have done that at a cheaper rate), but magnified it and made it illustrious. This circumstance did greatly magnify and advance his love, not only put it past dispute, but rendered it the object of the greatest wonder and admiration: "Now my creatures shall see that I love them, I will give them such an instance of it as shall be without parallel."

hill.scripture: Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends.
hill.text: Over the hill, John 15:13 shows what this love looks like when someone lays down his life for his friends. It is worth the walk.

scripture.16: For God so loved the world, that he gave his only born Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life.
scripture.17: For God didn’t send his Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world should be saved through him.
scripture.18: He who believes in him is not judged. He who doesn’t believe has been judged already, because he has not believed in the name of the only born Son of God.
